intro: A secret is any value whose disclosure lets someone act as you: an API key, a database password, a signing key, a session token. Secrets leak in boring ways — a commit, a log line, a screenshot, an environment dump in an error page — and the leak is usually discovered by an attacker first. This module is about the whole lifecycle: keeping secrets out of the places they leak from, storing and delivering them through a secrets manager, replacing long-lived secrets with short-lived ones wherever possible, rotating without downtime, and responding correctly when one gets out. The DevOps track introduced the tools; this module makes the practice systematic.
objectives: Identify every place a secret can leak and close the common ones (git, logs, images, tickets, CI output)
Deliver secrets to workloads from a secrets manager or KMS at runtime rather than baking them in
Replace static credentials with short-lived, identity-derived ones (cloud roles, OIDC, dynamic database credentials)
Rotate a secret without an outage using dual-validity
Run the response to a leaked secret in the right order

blocks.text: Secrets do not leak from vaults. They leak from the edges: a `.env` file added to git, a debug log that prints the request headers, a Docker layer that copied a key and "deleted" it in the next layer, a CI job that echoed its environment, a Slack message, a stack trace on an error page, a public object storage bucket with a config backup. Public repositories are scraped continuously; a cloud key pushed to GitHub is typically used within minutes.

rows: Pre-commit and CI secret scanning; `.gitignore` for env files; history rewrite is not enough, rotate
Never `COPY` secrets; multi-stage builds; use build secrets that do not persist in layers
Redact known secret shapes at the logger; generic error pages; never log headers or env
Masked secrets, no `env` dumps, forked PRs get no secrets
A policy plus a scanner; share via the secrets manager's link, not the value

blocks.caption: Find secrets before they are pushed: gitleaks as a pre-commit hook and in CI, scanning history as well as the working tree.
blocks.code:
# one-off scan of the whole history
gitleaks git --redact -v .

# pre-commit: block commits that contain a secret
cat > .pre-commit-config.yaml <<'EOF'
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.21.2
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks
EOF
pre-commit install

blocks.text: Removing a secret from a later commit changes nothing: the value is in the history and in every clone. A leaked secret is a compromised secret; the only fix is revocation and rotation.

sections.heading: A secrets manager, and how workloads get secrets

blocks.text: A **secrets manager** (a cloud provider's secrets service, HashiCorp Vault, or similar) stores secrets encrypted with a KMS-backed key, controls access with identity-based policy, logs every read, versions values so rotation can roll back, and can generate secrets on demand. The application authenticates to it with its workload identity (an instance role, a Kubernetes service account, an OIDC token) and fetches what it needs at startup or on demand. Nothing is stored in code, images or CI variables except the identity that is allowed to ask.

blocks.caption: Fetch at runtime with the workload's own identity; cache in memory; never write to disk or log.
blocks.code:
import json

import boto3

_client = boto3.client("secretsmanager")
_cache: dict[str, dict] = {}


def get_secret(name: str) -> dict:
    """Return the secret's JSON fields; the instance/pod role must allow secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on it."""
    if name not in _cache:
        resp = _client.get_secret_value(SecretId=name)
        _cache[name] = json.loads(resp["SecretString"])
    return _cache[name]


db = get_secret("prod/orders/db")
# db["username"], db["password"], db["host"] -> build the connection; do not print them

blocks.text: On Kubernetes the same pattern is a CSI secrets-store driver or an operator (External Secrets) that syncs from the manager into Secret objects, with the manager remaining the source of truth. Plain Kubernetes Secrets are base64, not encrypted, unless encryption at rest is configured for etcd; treat them as delivery, not storage. Mount secrets as files with restrictive permissions rather than environment variables where you can: environment variables are inherited by child processes and appear in crash dumps and debug endpoints.
Scope access by path and identity: the orders service can read `prod/orders/*` and nothing else. A single "app" role with read on everything turns one compromised pod into all your secrets.

The best secret is one that expires before it can be misused. Cloud instance and pod roles hand out credentials that rotate automatically every few hours. OIDC federation lets CI jobs exchange a signed job token for cloud credentials that last minutes. **Dynamic database credentials** go further: the secrets manager creates a database user with a lease when the application asks, and drops it when the lease expires, so there is no shared password to leak at all. Signed URLs and tokens with `exp` claims do the same for object access and APIs.

blocks.caption: Dynamic Postgres credentials from Vault: each request creates a fresh user that expires on its own.
blocks.code:
# configure once: how Vault connects, and a role that defines the SQL to create a user
vault write database/config/orders \
  plugin_name=postgresql-database-plugin \
  allowed_roles="orders-app" \
  connection_url="postgresql://{{username}}:{{password}}@db.internal:5432/orders" \
  username="vault" password="REPLACED_AFTER_ROTATE_ROOT"

vault write database/roles/orders-app \
  db_name=orders \
  creation_statements="CREATE ROLE \"{{name}}\" WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '{{password}}' VALID UNTIL '{{expiration}}'; \
    GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO \"{{name}}\";" \
  default_ttl="1h" max_ttl="24h"

# the application (authenticated by its identity) asks for credentials
vault read database/creds/orders-app
# username  v-k8s-orders-app-3Hx...   password  A1b...   lease_duration 1h

blocks.text: Where a static secret is unavoidable (a third-party API key, a legacy system password), shorten its life administratively: rotate it on a schedule, restrict where it can be used from (IP allow-lists, scoped permissions), and monitor its use so that use from a new place is an alert.

Rotation fails in production when it is treated as a single swap: the new value is written, every consumer that still holds the old one breaks. The safe pattern is **dual validity**: create the new credential while the old one still works, roll consumers over to the new one, verify nothing uses the old one, then revoke it. For signing keys the same idea is key identifiers: publish both keys, sign with the new, verify with either, retire the old after all tokens signed by it have expired.

items: Create the new secret (new key, new database user, new API key) alongside the old.
Store it as the new version in the secrets manager; consumers that fetch on start pick it up on their next restart, consumers with a refresh loop pick it up within minutes.
Roll consumers deliberately (rolling restart) and watch error rates and auth failures.
Check the audit log: no successful use of the old version for a full cycle.
Revoke the old secret. Keep the old version in the manager, disabled, for forensics.

blocks.text: Build consumers to handle rotation from the start: read secrets at startup, refresh on a timer or on an auth failure, and never cache a secret to disk. A service that needs a redeploy to pick up a new password will be the reason rotation is skipped.

sections.heading: When a secret leaks: the order of operations

blocks.text: Speed and order matter more than blame. Assume the secret has already been used. **Revoke or rotate first**, before investigating, because every minute it remains valid is a minute of attacker access. Then **audit**: search cloud and application logs for use of the credential since the earliest possible exposure, looking especially for use from unfamiliar sources. **Contain** what the audit shows: new keys created, resources touched, data read. **Fix the leak path** so it cannot recur (add the scanner, redact the logger). Finally **write it up** blamelessly; the person who leaked it and reported it fast did the right thing, and the process that let it happen is what needs to change.

blocks.caption: Auditing use of a leaked cloud key: who used it, from where, and what they did.
blocks.code:
# events by this access key in the last 24 hours (CloudTrail must be enabled)
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=AccessKeyId,AttributeValue=AKIAEXAMPLEKEY \
  --start-time "$(date -u -v-24H +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" \
  --query 'Events[].{time:EventTime,name:EventName,src:CloudTrailEvent}' --output json \
  | jq -r '.[] | "\(.time) \(.name) \(.src | fromjson | .sourceIPAddress)"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

blocks.text: Prepare the playbook before you need it: who can revoke which secret, where the audit logs are, which consumers must be restarted, and who is told. A leak handled in twenty minutes with a clear playbook is an incident; the same leak discovered a month later from a cloud bill is a breach.

practice.title: Scan, store, rotate, respond
steps: Run `gitleaks git` against a repository you own. If it finds anything real, rotate that secret now; then install the pre-commit hook and confirm a commit containing `AKIA` followed by sixteen uppercase characters is blocked.

Store a test secret in a secrets manager (cloud, or a local Vault dev server started with `vault server -dev`). Write a fifteen-line script that reads it at startup with the workload's identity and prints only the field names, never the values.
Create a second version of the secret. Modify the script to refresh on a 60-second timer and confirm it picks up the new version without a restart.
Implement dual validity for an HMAC signing key: store two keys with ids, sign with the newest, verify against both, then remove the old one and confirm old signatures fail.
Write the leak playbook for one real secret in your environment: revoke command, audit query, consumers to restart, who to inform. Keep it with the runbooks.
Grep your application logs for anything shaped like a token or key (`Bearer `, `AKIA`, `-----BEGIN`). Add redaction at the logger for the shapes you find.

pitfalls: Deleting a leaked secret from git and calling it handled; the value is in the history and in every clone.
Baking secrets into container images or AMIs, where they persist in every layer and every copy.
One broad secrets-read role for all services, so one compromised pod reads everything.
Rotating by overwriting the only value, then discovering which consumers cached the old one from the outage.
Storing Kubernetes Secrets in git in plain base64, believing base64 is encryption.
Investigating a leak before revoking; the attacker keeps working while you read logs.

quiz.q: A developer accidentally commits a cloud access key to a public repository and force-pushes a rewritten history ten minutes later. What is the correct first action?
options: Revoke the key immediately, then audit its use since the push
Confirm the history rewrite removed every trace of the key
Make the repository private while the team investigates
Add a pre-commit secret scanner so it cannot happen again
quiz.explain: Public repositories are scraped in real time, so the key must be assumed used. Revocation stops the damage; audit shows what happened. Rewriting history and making the repo private do not un-leak a value already copied; the scanner is the right follow-up, not the first step.

quiz.q: Which approach eliminates the shared database password rather than protecting it?
options: Dynamic credentials: the secrets manager creates a per-workload database user with a short lease on request
Storing the password in a secrets manager and rotating it every 90 days
Encrypting the password in the application's configuration file with a KMS key
Restricting which IP addresses may connect to the database with that password
quiz.explain: With dynamic credentials there is no long-lived password to leak; each user expires on its own. The other options reduce the risk of a static secret but keep it in existence.

quiz.q: A service reads its API key from the secrets manager once at startup and caches it in memory. During rotation, the operator writes the new key as the current version and revokes the old one immediately. What happens?
options: Running instances keep using the revoked key and fail until they are restarted; rotation needed a dual-validity window
Nothing; the secrets manager pushes the new value into the running process automatically
The service switches to the new key on its next request because the cache is invalidated by the manager
The old key remains valid for the provider's grace period, so no failures occur
quiz.explain: Startup-only readers hold the old value until restarted. Safe rotation keeps the old key valid while consumers roll to the new one, verifies via audit that the old one is unused, and only then revokes. Consumers should also refresh on a timer or on auth failure.

quiz.q: Why is mounting a secret as a file (mode 0400) generally preferred over passing it as an environment variable in a container?
options: Environment variables are inherited by child processes and show up in crash dumps, debug endpoints and `docker inspect`; a file is read only by the code that opens it
Files are encrypted by the container runtime while environment variables are stored in plaintext
Environment variables have a size limit that most secrets exceed
Kubernetes cannot inject Secret values into environment variables
quiz.explain: Environment leaks are a common source of exposure: subprocesses, diagnostic pages that print the environment, and container metadata all reveal them. A file with restrictive permissions is scoped to the process that reads it. Neither is encrypted by the runtime, and both mechanisms exist in Kubernetes.

quiz.q: A platform team gives every service the same secrets-manager role with read access to all paths, to simplify onboarding. What is the main risk?
options: One compromised service can read every secret in the environment, turning a small breach into a total one
The secrets manager will rate-limit the shared role and cause outages
Audit logs become unusable because reads cannot be attributed to a service
Rotation becomes impossible because all services must be restarted at once
quiz.explain: Least privilege for secrets means each identity reads only its own paths. A shared broad role removes the boundary between services, so the blast radius of any compromise is everything. Attribution suffers too, but the primary risk is total exposure.
